name: GS23645-VPA-1 Wells of Life: Sustainable Safe Water for Malawi
description: The Wells of Life – Sustainable Safe Water for Malawi is a voluntary carbon mitigation Programme of Activities (PoA) registered under the Gold Standard for the Global Goals (GS4GG), coordinated and managed by EOS Climate and Energy Ltd as the Coordinating and Managing Entity (CME). The Programme is designed to improve continuous access to safe and reliable drinking water in underserved communities in Malawi, while reducing greenhouse gas emissions associated with the boiling of drinking water using non-renewable biomass fuels. VPA-1, the first real case Voluntary Project Activity under the PoA, covers 19 solar-powered groundwater well systems implemented across the Southern Region of Malawi, spanning the districts of Machinga, Zomba, Mulanje, Thyolo, and Blantyre. The Programme applies the Safe Drinking Water Supply (SDWS v2.0) methodology and contributes to SDG 3, 5, 6, 7, 13, and 15. No financial burden is placed on end-users; access to safe drinking water is provided free of charge to beneficiary communities.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals
poa_project_name: EOS Climate – High-Integrity Climate & Social Impact Programme

name: EOS Climate – High-Integrity Climate & Social Impact Programme
description:
The EOS Climate – High-Integrity Climate & Social Impact Programme is a Programme of Activities (PoA) developed under the Gold Standard for the Global Goals (GS4GG) framework, aligned with the Paris Agreement. The Programme is coordinated and managed by EOS Climate as the Coordinating and Managing Entity (CME).
The Programme addresses greenhouse gas emissions associated with the use of non-renewable biomass fuels for boiling and sterilizing water in rural and peri-urban communities across Malawi. In the baseline scenario, households rely on unsafe water sources and boil water using firewood or charcoal, resulting in adverse health impacts, time burdens on women and children, local deforestation, and significant GHG emissions.
The Programme enables access to safe, reliable, and continuous drinking water through the installation of solar-powered artesian borehole systems with communal tap stands. All project activities operate with zero direct GHG emissions, eliminating the need for biomass combustion at the point of water use.
The geographical boundary is national in scope, covering eligible rural and peri-urban areas across Malawi. Individual Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs) are developed and included under the PoA framework over time, in accordance with Gold Standard requirements.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

name: GS23168-GS23169-OYU - Clean Water for Malawian Communities
description: The primary objective of this project is to rehabilitate broken and non-functional boreholes to provide clean and safe drinking water to local communities in Malawi. This initiative addresses the need for alternative water purification methods, reducing the reliance on boiling water for drinking purposes and thereby improving the living conditions of the population. The project alleviates the burden on rural women and children, who often bear the responsibility of collecting water and firewood by ensuring access to clean drinking water within 1 kilometre of households. Consequently, this project reduces carbon dioxide emissions associated with the combustion process traditionally used for water purification. In addition to its environmental impact, the project significantly enhances the quality of life, health, and socio-economic status of beneficiaries in the water-stressed regions of Malawi. It includes hygiene awareness campaigns to improve sanitation among local inhabitants. Furthermore, it creates employment opportunities for young people through installing and maintaining rehabilitated boreholes.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals
poa_project_name: OYU - Clean Water for Malawian Communities

description:

name: GS23612 - VPA-1 - Renewable energy generation through solar photovoltaic in Thailand
description:
The proposed VPA aims to increase renewable energy generation capacity via solar photovoltaic (PV) installation in public and private buildings. Thailand has immense potential for solar-based projects. While large-scale solar farms require large land-use, rooftop solar can utilize the space on the rooftops of buildings or in and around as captive ground-mounted solar installations within the premises of the buildings in cities. Thus, installing solar for buildings is a practical measure to reduce emissions and energy demand for cities.
The VPA entails the installation of rooftop and ground-mounted solar PV systems for captive (self-consumption) use in Thailand. The VPA will generate approximately 20,126 MWh annually and achieve 8,030 tCO2 in annual emission reductions.

name: Kuphatana - Acções Inclusivas para Florestas Sustentáveis ​​em Moçambique
description:
The Kuphatana project aims to reforest 1,000 hectares of highly degraded land in the Administrative Post of Murraça, Mozambique, to restore the local ecosystem and support the socio-economic development of nearby communities. The project adopts a participatory approach, integrating environmental restoration with diversified livelihood activities such as beekeeping and dried mango production to ensure long-term sustainability and community engagement.
Climate change mitigation/adaptation contributions
Carbon Sequestration: The project establishes a forest that serves as a carbon sink, sequestering an annual average of 8,925 tCO2e. Over the 40-year crediting period, the total estimated net benefit is 351,044.5 tCO2e.
Biodiversity Enhancement: By planting a mix of native species (Vachellia xanthophloea and Khaya anthotheca) alongside non-invasive Eucalyptus urophylla, the project restores habitats for local flora and fauna
Climate Adaptation through Livelihoods - Beekeeping: The project engages 15 families per year from adjacent villages, providing them with beehives and training. This creates a direct economic incentive for the community to protect the forest from threats such as uncontrolled fires or illegal deforestation, as the bee colonies rely on the trees for nectar.
Climate Adaptation through Livelihoods - Sustainable Value Chains: Establishing a local value chain for dried mangoes offers diversified, climate-resilient financial growth for local families.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

name: QSHM Cork Oak Afforestation 2026
description: Transformation of degraded land in Extremadura, Spain into cork oak estates. This project is the first in a series of future projects that will be grouped by annual cohorts. The baseline scenario is that traditional cork oak woodlands are under serious threats from climate change, fragile ecosystems, lack of management, wildfires as well as biotic and abiotic stresses. There is almost no incentive to plant new cork oak trees due to the very long time horizon. Cork oak estates increase the ecosystem value of the land, providing valuable habitats for native species, reducing erosion, and preserving the soil structure, increasing water holding and storing capacity as well as increasing shades. Degraded land is often used for non-permanent pastures, leading to desertification.

The B4H Initiative  is a sustainable energy project aimed at promoting renewable energy and waste management in rural households across two Indian states. The initiative involves the installation of 14,690 household biogas plants, primarily in Maharashtra (13,752 units) and Madhya Pradesh (938 units). These plants utilize animal dung to generate biogas for thermal energy, reducing greenhouse gas emissions and dependence on fossil fuels.

The project adheres to the "Methodology for Animal Manure Management and Biogas Use for Thermal Energy Generation" (Version 1.1, released January 25, 2023). The Household biogas units are sized at 2m³ , 3m³ , and 4m³, enabling clean cooking and organic fertilizer production for beneficiaries.

By addressing methane emissions from manure and providing affordable energy, B4H enhances livelihoods, improves air quality, and supports climate resilience in underserved communities. The initiative targets rural farmers, with installations verified through a detailed beneficiary database,to ensure long-term monitoring for carbon credit issuance.

The Project will provide safe water to communities in Rwanda by installing water treatment technologies (in-line chlorination) to existing community water supply (CWS) systems. name: Katunguru Restoration Project
description:
The project aims to restore 791 hectares of degraded land in the north-eastern section of Kibale National Park, Uganda. Following heavy encroachment in the past century, the area was abandoned but natural forest regeneration remains severely constrained by elephant grass and recurring fires. Without active intervention, forest recovery would not occur.

The project site is located in the mid-eastern part of Kibale National Park in Kyenjojo District, Western Uganda, and borders communities largely dependent on smallholder agriculture and affected by land scarcity, human–wildlife conflict, and pressure on natural resources.

Restoration will focus on active reforestation using indigenous tree species, including nursery establishment, seedling production and planting, weeding, fire prevention, patrolling, and long-term maintenance. Community members will be engaged through employment opportunities. Complementary activities will address human–wildlife conflict, support alternative livelihoods such as beekeeping, piggery, and agroforestry, and promote environmental awareness.

Without the project, the area would remain dominated by elephant grass and frequent fires, resulting in low carbon storage, limited biodiversity recovery, and soil degradation. The project changes this trajectory by enabling large-scale forest restoration, improving habitat quality, increasing carbon sequestration, and delivering socio-economic benefits to neighbouring communities.

name: QSHM Cork Oak Afforestation Pre 2026
description:
Transformation of degraded land in Extremadura, Spain into cork oak estates. This project is the first in a series of future projects that will be grouped by annual cohorts.

The baseline scenario is that traditional cork oak woodlands are under serious threats from climate change, fragile ecosystems, lack of management, wildfires as well as biotic and abiotic stresses. There is almost no incentive to plant new cork oak trees due to the very long time horizon.

Cork oak estates increase the ecosystem value of the land, providing valuable habitats for native species, reducing erosion, and preserving the soil structure, increasing water holding and storing capacity as well as increasing shades. Degraded land is often used for non-permanent pastures, leading to desertification.

name: Mechanical Reuse of Steel Plates from Wind Turbines
description: This project aims to mechanically process large-format steel plates (up to 2 t) from industrial dismantling without melting them down. The plates are restored to a technically flawless condition through straightening, flame cutting, and sandblasting, and are then reintroduced to the market as construction steel. In contrast to conventional recycling methods that rely on energy-intensive melting processes (e.g., blast furnaces or electric arc furnaces (EAF)), this project creates 'Reuse Steel' through a purely mechanical process. This approach avoids a significant portion of the energy and CO2 intensity associated with conventional steel production. The resulting Reuse Steel can be a substitute for various steel applications across construction or infrastructure components (non-structural).

name: Eternal Flame cooking bags
description:
69% of Lesotho’s population live rurally and cook on open fires. Cooking this way is hugely consumptive of wood, water and time. The purpose of the project is to reduce the negative impacts of cooking using biomass in Lesotho. Traditional foods such as beans require long cooking times, meaning large amounts of wood. A typical Lesotho household cooks continuously for 5 hours each day.

Fuel wood harvesting is hard, tiring and repetitive work often done by young women. This limits opportunities for education and independence, and exposes women to risk of assault. Harvesting also impacts local habitats and exposes soil to irreversible erosion. Water must also be collected, much of which is lost during the traditional cooking process.

In partnership with local women, we are making heat retention cooking bags. Instead of hours of continuous cooking, the bag only requires the cook to bring food to the boil then place the hot lidded pot into the bag. This reduces cooking time from hours to 25 minutes.

79% less fuel wood is required, equating to CO2e reduction of around two tonnes per bag per year. 80% less water is required as water no longer boils away during cooking, which also means nutrients are not lost, improving the nutritional value of the food.

Ultimately, the cook saves 1500 hours per year. It is no overstatement to say this changed lives in our pilot program. Women began craft making, trained to manufacture the Eco Cook Bags, or are growing and selling food.

name: BIOPLANTATION Ghana Regenerative Agroforestry Project
description: BIOPLANTATION is undertaking an agroforestry project in collaboration with local communities in Ghana. The project activity aims to restore degraded, under utilized land by developing biodiverse, regenerative agro forests. These forests will help combat climate change, support food security and create local jobs. The project will include Moringa Oleifera, a fast-growing and climate-resilient tree and associated species, along with local crops like peanuts and native species, to regenerate soil, store carbon, and support local livelihoods. BIOPLANTATION will bring together proven techniques, in a modular and regenerative design, that can be replicated and scaled up to different communities in Ghana. Planting of trees and crops including Moringa, peanuts, native fruits, fire/windbreak species, and aromatic plants. Soil restoration and regeneration will be through nitrogen-fixing plants and organic matter. Enhancing indigenous biodiversity will be by allocating 10% of project land to support pollination, biodiversity, and honey production.  BIOPLANTATION Ghana is committed to working in close partnership with local communities. During all phases of planning, implementation, and monitoring, community feedback and participation will be prioritized. The project will offer training, ownership, and income opportunities to local residents.

name: Smart Train Lease CO2 Reduction Project
description:
Smart Train Lease GmbH is a subsidiary of Siemens Mobility founded in 2023 and
launched to the market in February 2024 in Germany. Smart Train Lease offers the
opportunity to rent innovative, sustainable, state-of-the-art battery trains which can
replace diesel trains. Mireo Smart trains are part of the leasing model of Smart Train
Lease. They are available in various versions but for this project activity the focus is on
the highly energy-efficient battery-electric train (referred to as “Plus B”). The battery
train fleet is managed centrally and enables rail operators to rent trains at short notice, offering a cost-efficient solution for regional passenger transport services, depending
on the demand. production, lease and monitoring of 24 Mireo Smart Plus B across Germany, starting from 2026. The ultimate purpose of Smart Train Lease is to displace old

The objective of the program is to support smallholder farmers and rural communities in adopting sustainable agroforestry practices, which involve planting trees alongside crops or on fallow land across India. These activities will help restore soil health, improve agricultural productivity, and generate long-term environmental and economic benefits. 

Farmers will retain full ownership and rights over the trees they plant and the outputs from those trees. Any profits from the planting of additional species (such as fruit or timber trees) will belong entirely to the farmers. In addition to the economic benefits, the project will also reduce vulnerability to climate change. By increasing tree cover, it will help combat land degradation, improve water retention, and enhance biodiversity. Furthermore, the program will provide farmers access to carbon credit revenue share, promoting sustainable land use while improving their long-term livelihoods

name: CDR ORINOQUIA
description:
The CDR ORINOQUÍA project, developed by Biofix Consultoría S.A.S BIC, is a large-scale afforestation, reforestation, and revegetation (ARR) initiative designed to mitigate climate change by restoring degraded savannah ecosystems in the Orinoco region of Colombia. The project covers 8,441 hectares across seven private properties (Arizona, La Fortuna, La Carolina, San Andrés, Villa Claudia, Buenos Aires, and San Miguel) located in Puerto Gaitán, Meta.

The project employs a dual reforestation strategy:

Forest Plantations: Establishment of non-native species (Eucalyptus pellita and Pinus caribaea).

Natural Enrichment: Restoration of non-flood zones and flooded areas (gallery and moriche forests) using native species such as Cassia grandis, Hymenaea courbaril, Caraipa llanorum, Mauritia flexuosa, Euterpe precatoria, and Manilkara zapota.

To achieve its goals, the project operates a permanent nursery producing over three million seedlings annually. Implementation includes specialized machinery for site preparation, alongside GPS and drone technology for precise monitoring. This integrated approach aims to increase carbon sequestration and generate certified carbon credits while contributing to SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 8 (Decent Work), SDG 5 (Gender Equality) and SDG 15 (Life on Land). The project boundary encompasses all land parcels dedicated to these ARR activities as GHG sinks.

name: Green Mining’s GHG Emissions Reductions through Recycling in Brazil
description:
Green Mining's PoA is based on operationalizing the collection, transportation, and destination of waste for recycling. In doing so, the PoA promotes the circular economy and prevents the environmental impacts of manufacturing new products from virgin material, ensuring greater energy efficiency in the production process and, thus, reducing associated Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions.

The PoA is located in Brazil, and its operations are organized around receiving centers strategically placed in areas with high post-consumer waste generation. These centers receive, weigh, and properly store waste brought by registered local waste pickers, providing them fair compensation in a way that prioritizes the social inclusion of people in vulnerable situations.

In this regard, the PoA stands out for its disruptive nature, passing on the full value of waste to registered waste pickers and expanding the positive social impact of recycling.

Once properly registered, the waste is transported to the plants responsible for the recycling process, ensuring its subsequent reinsertion into the production chain.

This PoA constitutes, therefore, an overarching framework aimed at promoting recycling in Brazil in an inclusive and sustainable manner.

name: Alternative Fuel and Clinker Optimization Project
description:
The proposed project activity aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions at the Lam Thach Cement Plant through the introduction of alternative fuels and clinker optimization measures. The project will replace a portion of fossil fuels traditionally used in the cement kiln with waste-derived fuels such as refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and dewatered sludge, which would otherwise be landfilled or improperly disposed. This substitution reduces CO₂ emissions associated with fossil fuel combustion and supports improved waste management practices.

In addition, the project will lower process emissions by decreasing the clinker-to-cement ratio through the increased use of suitable supplementary cementitious materials. This results in reduced calcination-related CO₂ emissions from clinker production. The combined interventions contribute to a significant reduction in the carbon intensity of cement manufacturing at Lam Thach.

The initiative supports Vietnam’s climate and circular economy objectives by diverting waste from landfills, reducing fossil fuel dependence, and promoting more efficient resource use. The overall project activity contributes to regional and national sustainable development.

name: US SecondCropTM Microbial Carbon Removal (USSC24)
description:
Overview
The US SecondCropTM Microbial Carbon Removal project represents a pioneering
approach in agriculture-based carbon removal and is centered around the use of
proprietary microbial technology to improve soil health and drive long-term carbon
sequestration. The project transforms conventional farmland into durable carbon sinks
by enhancing stable soil carbon, producing measurable climate and soil health outcomes.
A key innovation in this program is the deployment of CarbonBuilderTM, a proprietary
microbial inoculant developed by Loam Bio (refer to Appendix 5 - CarbonBuilder
Development Stages at Loam Bio for a detailed summary of the product development
pipeline). CarbonBuilder is applied as a seed treatment to enhance plant fertility,
promote soil health, and increase the sequestration of soil organic carbon by
reintroducing beneficial fungi into the soil. The US SecondCrop Microbial Carbon Removal
project represents a grouped project comprising 36 farms. Participating farms are
located in Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, South Dakota and Wisconsin with a
median farm size of 550 acres. All farms in the project are historically and currently used
for cropping, primarily under a corn-soy rotation.
Prior to the implementation of this project, there were no equivalent initiatives in the
region focused on stable soil organic carbon sequestration. Agricultural practices in the
U.S. Midwest were predominantly conventional, characterized by routine tillage and
heavy reliance on synthetic fertilizers. The baseline scenario assumes the continuation of
these practices in the absence of the project, leading to higher emissions and declining
soil resilience over time. Under the project, participating farmers apply CarbonBuilder to
applicable crops each year at the time of planting. Unlike conventional soil carbon
projects that depend only on practice changes (no-till, cover crops), Loam’s inoculant

accelerates microbial-fungal-root interactions that channel plant carbon into mineral-
associated organic matter (MAOM) and aggregate-associated organic matter.
Building stronger soil health in agricultural landscapes within United
States
Regenerative agricultural practices hold immense potential for higher adoption rates
among farmers in the U.S. Midwest, a region characterized by its flat topography and
fertile mollisol soils that are ideal for large-scale, mechanized farming (USDA NRCS).
Historically, conventional farming in this area has relied on intensive tillage and heavy
use of synthetic fertilizers to maximize yields. However, this has led to higher emissions and declining soil resilience over time. A study in the journal Earth's Future found that
agricultural fields in the Midwestern U.S. have lost an average of two millimeters of soil
per year since Euro-American settlement, nearly double the rate the USDA considers
sustainable. It has been estimated that over the last 160 years, the region has lost
approximately 57.6 trillion metric tons of topsoil, with plowing activities cited as the
major culprit (Thaler et al. 2022). Similarly, research published in the Proceedings of the
National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) revealed that the Midwest Corn Belt has lost its
topsoil (A-horizon soil) from roughly one-third of its cultivated area, a significantly
higher estimate than previous soil surveys indicated. This soil loss has removed 1.4 ±
0.5 petagrams of carbon from hillslopes, reducing crop yields in the study area by
around 6% and causing billions in annual economic losses (Thaler et al. 2021). Poor soil
health has a significant impact on productivity and the broader agricultural economy.
The shift to regenerative practices including reduced or no-tillage, cover cropping, and
the use of bio-stimulants, is therefore crucial for improving soil health, enhancing water
retention, and mitigating climate change through potential widespread carbon removal
and long-term sequestration. The SecondCrop Microbial Carbon Removal project is
designed to accelerate this transition by making it easier for farmers to adopt these
practices over a sustained period.
Microbial seed technology and development of CarbonBuilder
CarbonBuilder harnesses the interactions between beneficial fungi, plants and soil. With
CarbonBuilder, beneficial fungi are reintroduced into soils that have been stripped of
their native fungal communities due to harsh cropping systems. These fungi enhance
natural carbon deposition into stable aggregates and mineral associated forms and
promote long-term retention of carbon in the soil. Loam's approach is rooted in
extensive research and development. The company has collaborated with leading
academic institutions, including the University of Sydney, Australian National University,
Western Sydney University, University of Newcastle, University of Queensland, and
Lawrence Livermore to deepen its understanding of plant-fungi-soil interactions in the
development of CarbonBuilder. CarbonBuilder represents our patented use of Dark
Septate Endophytes (DSE) to establish symbiotic relationships with plant roots resulting
in the extension of fungal networks that improve nutrient uptake, enhance soil structure,
and increase carbon deposition. The fungi within CarbonBuilder actively deposit carbon
into stable soil aggregates and bind it to mineral surfaces increasing the mean residence
time in the soil from weeks or months to decades or even centuries. In addition,
replicated small-plot field trials hold a pivotal place in Loam’s CarbonBuilder product
development process. These trials have allowed us to methodically evaluate
CarbonBuilder's impact on crop yield, soil health, and carbon sequestration. The data generated from these trials enabled Loam to identify the most promising products, which
then progressed to strip trials on farms.
Loam Bio patented technology and geographic operations
Loam Bio and its CarbonBuilder products are USDA compliant to be utilised on-farm in
the United States (South Dakota, Nebraska, Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri, Mississippi,
Arizona; with approvals pending in Ohio, Colorado and Idaho.). To date, Loam Bio has
been successfully granted 10 patents covering fungal compositions and microbial
mixtures isolated in United States and Australia and their methods of use within Loam’s
bioproduction operations. These fungal strains are active ingredients in CarbonBuilder’s
product line which are available for use as eligible management practices under the
SecondCrop program. Loam Bio, LLC continues to actively build out its patent pipeline,
with over 30 patents that have been filed within jurisdictions of Australia, Brazil, Canada
and United States.
Loam Bio as project developer
Loam Bio is the project developer, technology provider, and market lead of the US
SecondCrop Microbial Carbon Removal project. Loam Bio produces and delivers the
microbial inoculant, supports farmers with practice adoption, and manages the soil
carbon project. The Loam Commercial Operation team oversees project enrollment and
eligibility verification, data collection and ongoing project monitoring, and facilitation of
credit issuance.
Estimated scale of carbon dioxide removal
It is estimated that the grouped project will achieve an average annual removal of 1.2
tonnes of CO2e per acre. Over the initial five-year crediting period, the project is
expected to remove approximately 126,745 tCO2e. By offering farmers a new, low-effort
tool to build stable soil carbon, the project aims to contribute significantly to climate
change mitigation while fostering more resilient and profitable agricultural practices. The
use of CarbonBuilder is a practice that meets additionality requirements without
requiring farmers to make extensive changes to their existing operations. These
outcomes underscore the project’s significant contribution to climate mitigation, while
also advancing sustainable and regenerative agricultural practices across the U.S.
Midwest.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

name: Small Farmers' Carbon Farming Project in Chishang, Taiwan
description:
Chishang, nestled in Taitung County, Taiwan, is renowned as a premier rice production region with a legacy of more than 70 years. The area’s lush paddies and traditional agricultural rhythms are stewarded by the Wanan Community Development Association (WACDA), an active local group established three decades ago. WACDA’s mission centers on environmental protection, cultural conservation, and the promotion of organic farming—principles that have guided community action and land management for generations.
Typical farming practices in Chishang after the second rice harvest in late October include thorough removal of litter and several rounds of tillage, followed by maintaining clear, fallow fields until February. This period of rest for the land helps sanitize soil-borne disease bacteria. However, to manage weeds during this time, herbicides have traditionally been applied, reflecting both pragmatic and conventional approaches to field management.
In recent years, Chishang’s farmers, under WACDA’s leadership, have begun to embrace more sustainable soil management techniques. Inspired by the Gold Standard for Global Goals (GS4GG) Soil Organic Carbon Framework Methodology, the community has adopted Cover Crops and Improved Tillage Activity Modules. These practices promise enhanced outcomes for both food security and climate resilience, by increasing soil carbon, reducing chemical use, and supporting ecosystem health.

description:
The goal of the “Community Program for the Preservation and Restoration of Mangroves” is to implement projects for the restoration of degraded mangrove and coastal/freshwater wetlands ecosystems. The aim is to recover ecological functionality by re-establishing hydrological connectivity, improving biodiversity, and removing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) through natural carbon sequestration processes.
VPAs included under the PoA will be selected where degradation is demonstrated and restoration is technically feasible, prioritizing actions such as hydrological reconnection, assisted natural regeneration, and targeted enrichment planting with native species, together with the maintenance and monitoring required for durable outcomes. The aim is to restore ecological processes (water exchange, sediment dynamics, recruitment), enhance biodiversity, and remove CO₂ through conservative, verified sequestration in line with Gold Standard requirements.

description:
Carbon Neutral Energy Systems Limited (C-NES) has developed the Ecofoyer Guinée – Programme for the Dissemination of Improved and Advanced Cookstoves in Guinea as a Gold Standard Programme of Activities (PoA). The PoA reduces greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and improve household well-being by displacing traditional, inefficient biomass cookstoves with modern, energy-efficient, and cleaner alternatives.

Through the dissemination of Improved Cookstoves (ICS), Advanced Cookstoves (ACS), and the local production of renewable biomass fuels (pellets), the Ecofoyer Guinée PoA contributes to sustainable energy access, climate change mitigation, and socio-economic development across urban, peri-urban, and rural areas of Guinea.

VPA 01, implemented under this PoA, covers the prefectures of Conakry, N’Zérékoré, Forécariah, and Beyla. The activity involves the dissemination, monitoring, and maintenance of ICS and ACS technologies, as well as the introduction of locally manufactured biomass pellets as a renewable fuel alternative. Implementation will be carried out through partnerships with Local Implementation Partners (LIPs) responsible for distribution, user training, awareness campaigns, and after-sales support.

This first VPA serves as the real-case example for the PoA, demonstrating the operational model, monitoring framework, and sustainable development co-benefits expected from future VPAs to be included under the Ecofoyer Guinée Programme.

name: CCT Clean Cooking Project, Tanzania
description:
This Gold Standard Large-Scale (Individual) Project Activity is a voluntary initiative developed by Clean Cooking Technologies S.R.L. (CCT) as the Project Developer. The project will be supported by multiple investors and funding partners. The Host Country for this project is the United Republic of Tanzania, where the activity will be implemented across the country.

The project aims to distribute high-quality induction stoves and electric pressure cookers (collectively referred to as electric cookstoves) to households and communities in Tanzania. Implementation will be led by CCT Tanzania, in collaboration with local organizations. The project will initially be rolled out in Dar es Salaam and subsequently expanded to other regions across Tanzania based on demand.

In Tanzania, a large proportion of households continue to rely on inefficient traditional cooking methods—such as three-stone fires and traditional charcoal stoves—that consume significant amounts of biomass and contribute to deforestation and indoor air pollution. By introducing modern, energy-efficient electric cooking technologies, the project seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, improve indoor air quality, and enhance the overall quality of life for participating households.

The project will be implemented in both rural and urban areas where households have access to electricity.  The project will have a total crediting period of 15 years, comprising an initial 5-year period with two renewals of 5 years each.                                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     100 of % distributed induction stoves in the project will be equipped with IoT devices to enable continuous monitoring of energy consumption for cooking and water heating in the households. The project will apply the Gold Standard-approved methodology, "Methodology for Metered & Measured Energy Cooking Devices" (Version 1.2), recognized as the most robust and conservative emission reduction calculation approach for cookstove carbon projects. This methodology is also endorsed by the ICVCM under its Core Carbon Principles (CCP), ensuring transparency and integrity in carbon credit issuance from cookstove projects.

By combining energy-efficient modern elelctric cookstove technology with real-time usage monitoring using the latest IoT device and a rigorous Gold Standard Metered Methodology, and further fNRB value derived from MoFUSS for Tanzania, the project will generate high-quality, high-integrity carbon credits while avoiding any risk of overestimation. The project is also one of the approved project by Sylvera.  

Beyond emissions reduction, the project is designed to deliver substantial co-benefits aligned with many UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including:
- SDG 1: No Poverty
- SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being
- SDG 4: Quality Education
- SDG 5: Gender Equality
- SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy
- SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic Growth
- SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production
- SDG 13: Climate Action
- SDG 15: Life on Land
These co-benefits will be formally certified under the Gold Standard framework, reinforcing the project's holistic impact on climate and community resilience.

name: Developing sustainable rice value chains for   smallholder farmers in Dong Thap from 2022 –  2035
description:
This project introduces Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) as a climate-smart water management practice in rice farming in Dong Thap Province, a major rice-producing area of the Mekong Delta. The project aims to reduce methane emissions from rice cultivation, save irrigation water, and support sustainable rice production. It is being implemented by Rikolto in Vietnam acting on behalf of Livelihoods Carbon Fund (LCF3).
The core technical intervention of the project is the application of AWD, a water-saving irrigation technique that reduces methane emissions in rice cultivation. Instead of keeping rice paddies continuously flooded, AWD involves allowing the field to dry intermittently, typically until the water level drops 15 cm below the soil surface, at which point irrigation is resumed with a shallow flood of 2–5 cm. This practice reduces the anaerobic conditions in the soil that are responsible for methane generation, without negatively affecting rice yields. 
To support this method, the project installs PVC monitoring tubes (commonly known as pani-pipes) in farmers’ fields. These tools allow farmers to visually monitor the water level in the soil and make informed irrigation decisions, making AWD both accessible and easy to implement.
In addition to water management, the project promotes improved straw and fertilizer practices. Rather than incorporating straw into the soil, which significantly contributes to methane emissions, farmers are encouraged to remove, compost, or repurpose straw for other uses such as mushroom cultivation. Fertilizer use is also optimized to improve nitrogen efficiency and reduce emissions of nitrous oxide (N₂O), another potent greenhouse gas.

name: GHG Emissions Reduction & Sequestration - Afforestation/Reforestation - Future Radici (Lanuvio-Roma-Lazio)
description:
The Real Case VPA Future Radici, Lanuvio represents a pivotal and strategic initiative within the broader framework of the Programme of Activities (PoA) Future Radici. Located in the municipality of Lanuvio (Rome), the project spans a total area of 403.9 hectares across three agricultural estates: Solonio, Presciano, and Campoleone. These lands are owned by Leone Alato SpA. The project envisions the planting of approximately 422,000 trees, with the goal of transforming these agricultural lands into thriving, biodiverse forest ecosystems.
The primary objective of the Real Case of Lanuvio is to establish native and ecologically rich forest environments through a combination of afforestation and agroforestry practices. These practices are carefully tailored to the pedoclimatic and ecological characteristics of each site, ensuring that the interventions enhance biodiversity, support complex habitats, and maximize long-term carbon sequestration. The forest models adopted in this project are non-extractive, the harvesting of timber or biomass is explicitly excluded. This commitment extends for a minimum duration of 60 years.
To quantify the carbon absorption, the project will rely on methodologies recommended by the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change). These methods will be calibrated using national and regional data. The goal is to produce credits that are measurable, verifiable, and directly linked to positive outcomes in both biodiversity and social impact.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

name: FS BECCS Project
description:
The FS BECCS project, proposed under the Gold Standard for Global Goals (GS4GG), reflects FS – Fueling Sustainability’s ambition to lead Brazil’s energy transition with innovation, technical excellence, and private investment. Founded in 2017, FS is the third-largest ethanol producer in the country, operating modern plants in Mato Grosso.

At its Lucas do Rio Verde facility, FS will capture biogenic CO₂ from corn ethanol fermentation. The stream, with about 98% purity, will be compressed, dehydrated, and injected into deep geological formations of the Parecis Basin for secure, long-term storage. As this CO₂ originates from the atmosphere via photosynthesis, its storage delivers net carbon removals.

Project development followed four phases: Phase 1 (2019–2020) confirmed storage potential through feasibility studies and 2D seismic data. Phase 2 (2020–2022) added a 3D seismic survey and design of capture and compression systems. Phase 3 (2022–2024) drilled a stratigraphic well, collected geological data, and began equipment procurement. Phase 4 (2024–2026), now underway, includes injectivity tests, well conversion, monitoring infrastructure, and capture system construction. Commercial operations are expected in 2025, with carbon injection June 2026.

name: BIWACALI
description:
BIWACALI stands for Burka Initiative for Water Balancing, Carbon Sequestration and Livelihood Improvement. The Oromo word “Burquaa” means “burbling spring”, symbolizing the main objective of this project: ensuring the water security of the West-Ethiopian Upper Dabana - and the East-Ethiopian Hakim Gara watersheds by restoring about 10,000 ha areas degraded area into forest over the next decades. This will be achieved by tree planting and applying the Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) technique, which is designed to significantly improve the income and livelihoods of local farming communities. 

Next to the physical restoration work, major project activities are the formation of cooperatives and unions for forest management and training on FMNR, sustainable farming methods and alternative livelihoods. The newly created cooperatives will be strongly supported by World Vision Ethiopia in the first years of the project. It is envisioned that afterwards, they will take on the main responsibility for managing the forest areas, their products and the monitoring of the project impacts. 

The project is being implemented jointly by the local communities, Heineken Ethiopia, World Vision Ethiopia and FORLIANCE.

name: GS23399 VPA-1 Renewable Biomass Briquette Production for Clean Energy
description: The proposed project involves the production and supply of approximately 10,200 tonnes of biomass briquettes annually, with the objective of replacing conventional fossil fuels such as coal, furnace oil, and firewood that are commonly used by industries and institutions for thermal energy applications. The primary goal is to promote the use of clean, renewable, and sustainable biomass energy while reducing reliance on carbon-intensive fuels. These briquettes are manufactured using agricultural residues and other organic biomass waste, which are typically discarded or left to decompose, resulting in methane emissions and environmental degradation. By converting this waste into high-density fuel briquettes, the project addresses key environmental and economic challenges. It contributes to greenhouse gas emission reductions by displacing fossil fuels and preventing methane emissions from un-managed biomass waste. The initiative also supports improved waste management through the productive use of agricultural residues, offers access to cleaner-burning fuels for small and medium-sized industrial units, and generates local employment across the biomass value chain—from raw material collection and processing to transportation and distribution. Additionally,by reducing the use of coal and wood, the project helps improve air quality and public health through lower emissions of particulate matter and other harmful pollutants.

This project aims to reduce methane (CH4) emissions through improved water management practices involving alternate wetting and drying (AWD) of the paddy lands. Rice is the most prominent food crop in India. It is the backbone of livelihood for millions of rural households and plays a vital role in the country’s food security. India is one of the world's largest producers and exporters of rice and hence plays an important part in the country’s economy. The proposed VPA activity is planned to be implemented in the Madhya Pradesh State of India.

name: GS PoA for Sustainable Rice Cultivation Projects in India
description: This is a Programme of Activities (PoA) called “GS PoA for Sustainable Rice Cultivation Projects in India” in India that will include various Voluntary Project Activities (VPAs) in it. The “GS PoA for Sustainable Rice Cultivation Projects in India” consists of implementation of Alternate and Wetting and Drying (AWD) practice in India. Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) method and aerobic rice cultivation method is a scientifically proven way of managing rice fields for better water management and achieving reduction or avoidance of methane emissions that is caused in traditional submerged rice fields. name: Avoiding methane emissions through composting at DN Agrar, Romania
description:
The “Avoiding Methane Emissions through Composting at DN Agrar, Romania” project aims to significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions by implementing controlled aerobic composting of raw dairy manure at two farms located in Alba and Hunedoara counties. Traditionally, manure is managed through open stockpiling or storage in lagoons, practices that lead to uncontrolled anaerobic decomposition and the release of methane (CH₄), a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential significantly higher than CO₂.

By diverting manure from these conventional methods and instead processing it through a structured composting system, the project prevents methane emissions at source. The composting process stabilizes the organic material, producing high-quality compost that can be applied to agricultural land. This not only improves soil health and fertility but also enhances the soil’s carbon sequestration capacity, supporting long-term climate resilience in Romanian agriculture.

In summary, the project delivers both immediate climate benefits through methane avoidance and broader environmental co-benefits by promoting sustainable manure management and improving local soil systems.

name: METHANE EMISSION REDUCTION BY AWD IN RICE FARMING IN CAMBODIA-VPA02
description: This VPA aims to save water and reduce methane emissions during rice farming by introducing water management technology to rice farming, which is one of the main greenhouse gas emission sources in Takeo of Cambodia. By participating in this project, farmers can produce low-carbon rice without reducing rice productivity and participate in mitigating climate change. ThanksCarbon, a business developer, has introduced an AI-based satellite technology into this project to reduce the burden on individual farmers for data collection and improve the convenience of monitoring data collection and MRV transparency. Farmers will be motivated and trained to refrain from continuously flooding their fields by putting the suggested AWD technology into effect, which would cut down on the quantity of CH4 emissions that would have been produced in the baseline situation. The sole change made to the project scenario is the adoption of alternating wetting and drying conditions rather than the submerged condition. Other than that, the project keeps the current agricultural techniques in place and does not introduce any new activities that might increase greenhouse gas emissions.

description:
The Ugum Watershed Reforestation and Carbon Offset Initiative targets 100 acres (~40.5 hectares) of degraded, non-forested savanna land in Southern Guam, within the villages of Inalåhan and Talo’fo’fo’. While the site has been undergoing restoration since 2019 under the Guam Restoration of Watersheds (GROW) initiative, only plantings occurring after April 7, 2023 are eligible for carbon crediting under this project.

Restoration activities reduce erosion, improve water quality, and enhance forest cover to buffer against the region’s susceptibility to fire, storm events, and flash flooding.

name: Producción sostenible de biofertilizantes y biogás a partir de desechos de materia orgánica. Gran Canaria
description:
The plant, located in the municipality of Agüimes, in Gran Canaria, is expected to come into operation in October 2025, at which time a three-month operational test phase will be carried out to guarantee the efficiency and safety of the process. The implementation to obtain emission reductions is estimated in the first quarter of 2026.
This first plant will be located next to the Southeast treatment plant, in the port free zone of Gran Canaria, which will facilitate its logistical integration and connectivity with distribution channels. It will be designed to manage up to 31,000 tonnes of organic waste per year, from which approximately 2,242 tonnes of biomethane per year will be produced, equivalent to 31,141 MWh of energy. This production of this energy vector represents a sustainable alternative to about 2,832 tons of propane gas, which will allow a significant reduction in the use of fossil fuels and polluting gas emissions and contribute to local climate and energy governance. 
As for the size and scope of the activity of the facility, it is estimated that it can serve some 45-65 hotels since the capacity of the digester, is 31,000 t/y of organic waste.
Among the key components of the project, the production of biomethane as a renewable substitute for propane gas and diesel stands out.

description:
The proposed initiative is a Voluntary Project Activity (VPA) focused on agroforestry plantations, to be implemented in Odisha, India. Implemented by the SGI Foundation, the project aims to sequester atmospheric carbon dioxide through large-scale plantation activities, while simultaneously enhancing local biodiversity, improving soil health, and promoting sustainable livelihoods. The project emphasizes the cultivation of native and climate-resilient agroforestry species such as Mango, Teak, Cashew, Jackfruit, Guava, and other regionally suitable trees under the first VPA. Active participation from local farmers is central to the initiative, empowering them to adopt agroforestry practices that improve income security and resilience to climate variability.
Beyond its environmental benefits, the project contributes significantly to socio-economic development by generating temporary employment for community members during the plantation's establishment and maintenance phases. It also strengthens long-term sustainability through capacity-building and inclusive community engagement. The initiative supports multiple SDGs, including Climate Action (SDG 13), Life on Land (SDG 15), and No Poverty (SDG 1), by integrating carbon sequestration with biodiversity conservation and rural development. A core objective of the project is to quantify the carbon sequestration potential of agroforestry plantations in Odisha while uplifting farming communities through sustainable land-use practices.

description:

The project intends to accelerate access to clean cooking by displacing use of inefficient biomass cooking devices and polluting fuels. Use of the project technology will displace GHG emissions from the thermal energy consumption required for cooking by households. This will consequently contribute towards reduced household air pollution and support several sustainable development goals. The project’s primary target is end-users who cook using inefficient biomass cookstoves and polluting fuels such as kerosene both in the urban and rural areas of Kenya.

Goals and Objectives of the Project Activity
According to the 2022 KNBS Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) report, 68.5% of Kenyan population still highly dependent on traditional cooking fuels, with firewood being the predominant cooking fuel. name: Ghana Cocoa Agroforestry Livelihoods Project
description:
The Ghana Cocoa Agroforestry Livelihoods Project is designed to enhance the productivity and long-term sustainability of cocoa farming systems while improving the livelihoods of the communities that depend on them. By introducing an agroforestry model that integrates shade tree species into existing cocoa plantations, the project aims to extend the productive lifespan of cocoa trees and strengthen the system’s resilience to environmental challenges, including pests and diseases. This initiative will be carried out in close partnership with the local communities, with a focus on engaging youth teams to lead on the ground implementation. 
The project is expected to reach 11,000 farmers for an implementation area of 17,000 hectares. The project’s main activity consists of planting shade and fruit trees within the existing cocoa plantations. Nine different native tree species will be incorporated into the farms to achieve a target density of 90 shade trees per hectare. 
Additionally, the new tree plantations will be associated with the training and coaching of the farmers in sustainable agroforestry practices such as tree management, pruning and Integrated Pest Management (IPM). The implementation of these practices is expected to increase the productive lifetime of the cocoa species and reduce the incidence of pests and diseases on the targeted trees. The project is expected to sequester 2.61 MtCO2e within 30 years.

name: Sterling Improved Cookstoves Carbon Project
description: In most of the countries on the African continent including Ghana, cooking is done on either 3-stone fires or very inefficient traditional cookstoves, consuming a lot of fuel, in particular non-renewable firewood and charcoal. The high biomass consumption has negative impacts on the environment leading to deforestation and land degradation, Greenhouse Gas Emissions (GHG) emissions, loss of soil fertility and soils’ reduced ability of water retention. Further, indoor air pollution through health-damaging pollutants while combusting firewood and charcoal result in diseases like e.g. pneumonia, stroke, ischemic heart diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases and lung cancer. The purpose of a ‘STERLING IMPROVED COOKSTOVES PROJECT Carbon Project Activities included under the Gold Standard’, is to disseminate highly efficient improved cookstoves (ICS to urban, peri-urban and/or rural users (households, communities, institutions, or SMEs) in Ghana. Several greenhouse gases (GHG), including carbon dioxide, are produced as a result of the incomplete combustion of biomass as used in cook stoves. More GHG emissions result from the use of biomass which is non-renewable. ICS improves heat transfer efficiency as compared to the baseline traditional cook stoves, thereby reducing both the amount of woody biomass used by unit appliances implemented and the emission of GHGs.

name: Project Saladillo: Sustainable Mosaic Afforestation Operation in Eastern Paraguay
description:
Project Saladillo transforms 15,946 hectares of cattle grazing land, subject to continual slash-and-burn practices, in Paraguay’s Cordillera region into a mosaic plantation combining commercial and conservation forestry. It prioritises long-term ecological resilience and sustainable development. The project integrates 25% permanent conservation with 75% selectively harvested forestry, maintaining at least 96% continuous forest cover. This model prevents deforestation by producing sustainable timber and biomass, while enhancing biodiversity through protection of native forests and riparian corridors, supporting habitat continuity and safeguarding local fauna.
An estimated 1,122,437 tons of CO₂ will be sequestered over 50+ years. High-precision carbon monitoring uses LiDAR-based models calibrated with field sampling to ensure accuracy in both accessible and remote areas.
Saladillo generates formal, year-round employment through staggered planting and harvesting, eliminating informal labour, reducing seasonal risks, and ensuring steady income for local communities. It collaborates closely with local NGOs such as Fundación Moisés Bertoni and the University of Asunción, integrating community engagement, biodiversity monitoring, and academic research.
The project adheres to the highest environmental and social safeguards, aligning with FSC certification, IFC Performance Standards, and World Bank guidelines, contributing to SDGs 8, 12, 13, and 15.

name: Niger Delta Community-Driven Mangrove Restoration [Regular VPA 1]
description: The Niger Delta Community-Driven Mangrove Restoration Project is a scalable initiative focused on restoring the historically mangrove-rich wetlands of the Niger Delta through a community-led approach. The Niger Delta—the largest river delta in Africa and home to the world’s third-largest mangrove forest—has faced severe degradation over the past decades due to a variety of pressures. This has compromised biodiversity, diminished livelihoods, and increased vulnerability to flooding and erosion for the 30 million people who live there. This project aims to restore the ecosystem through training local communities to plant native, locally adapted mangrove species, while also addressing the causes of mangrove loss. Its objectives are to: • Empower communities by providing the livelihood support, education, and tools needed to become long-term ecosystem stewards and bolster their resilience in a climate-changing world, • Restore a critical ecosystem and its services while promoting biodiversity by rebuilding the habitats of numerous species, strengthening regional food security, and providing flood and storm protection. • And finally, sequester carbon in the fight against climate change while utilizing mangroves as a powerful nature-based solution. Rooted in strong local partnerships and ecosystem restoration approaches, the project is designed to scale and serve as a model for community-first restoration across Nigeria and the wider region.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals
poa_project_name: Niger Delta Community-Driven Mangrove Restoration Project

name: Empowering Communities Through Improved Cookstoves
description: The Empowering Communities Through Improved Cookstoves project in rural Togo distributes fuel-efficient improved cookstoves (ICS) to replace traditional, inefficient three-stone fires commonly used in rural households. The cookstoves are manufactured locally in Togo, supporting infrastructure development, generating employment, and stimulating economic growth in the region. By reducing the amount of firewood required for cooking, the project alleviates the time and physical burden of firewood collection—a task that disproportionately falls on women and girls. This, in turn, enables greater access to education and income-generating opportunities. In addition to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, the project delivers a range of co-benefits, including: Improved indoor air quality, reducing the incidence of respiratory and eye-related illnesses caused by smoke inhalation from traditional stoves. Reduced pressure on local forests through decreased firewood demand, slowing deforestation and preserving biodiversity. Lower household expenditure on cooking fuel due to more efficient wood use. Increased time savings for women and children, enabling greater focus on education, caregiving, and economic activities. Job creation and skill development through local cookstove production and distribution. By addressing both climate change and local development needs, the project contributes to eight Sustainable Development Goals.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals
poa_project_name: Resilient Futures: Building Resilience to Poverty and Climate Change

name: Resilient Futures: Building Resilience to Poverty and Climate Change
description:
The “Resilient Futures” Programme of Activities (PoA) is a community-driven initiative designed to address the interlinked challenges of poverty, environmental degradation, and climate change across vulnerable rural regions. By deploying scalable, high-impact interventions—such as improved cookstoves, safe water technologies, biochar production, and regenerative agroforestry—this PoA aims to reduce and remove greenhouse gas emissions while strengthening the adaptive capacity of local communities.

Led by trusted local partners and supported by ethical climate finance, the PoA empowers women, improves health outcomes, restores ecosystems, and increases household income and food security. 

This programme contributes to multiple Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), SDG 5 (Gender Equality), SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 15 (Life on Land). 
The PoA is designed to enable the rapid scaling of ethical, verifiable carbon projects in West Africa and beyond—delivering measurable climate impact and real, lasting change for people and planet.

name: Landfill gas recovery, energy generation and  biogas distribution from CTR Santa Rosa
description:
1. Project Design and Scenarios
The project aims to collect and treat landfill gas (Landfill Gas – LFG) in various scenarios to reduce methane emissions. The planned scenarios include:
•Controlled flaring of collected gas;
•Supplying treated gas to industrial, commercial, or residential consumers;
•Using gas as fuel for electricity generation.
These scenarios will be applied according to the specific characteristics and needs of each landfill included in the program.
At the Santa Rosa Waste Treatment Center (CTR) in Seropédica (Rio de Janeiro – Brazil), the current scenario involves the capture of landfill gas (LFG) for combustion and distribution to external consumers. In the future, infrastructure is planned for electricity generation from the collected gas.
2. Technologies and Measures
The project uses modern technologies for LFG capture, treatment, and utilization, such as:
•Vertical and horizontal wells for gas collection;
•High-efficiency flaring systems;
•Infrastructure for gas treatment, including contaminant removal;
•Infrastructure for transporting biogas by trucks for external thermal applications.
For future phases, CTR Santa Rosa also plans to install modular equipment for electricity generation.
Additionally, the project includes strict monitoring to ensure operational efficiency and safety.
3. Geographic Boundaries
Currently, the project only includes CTR Santa Rosa in Seropédica/RJ. Geographic coordinates: -22.795703 (latitude) and -43.760558 (longitude).
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

The primary objective of this project is to contribute to the development of Nicaragua's electricity sector while adhering to sustainability principles and fostering the transformation of the country's energy matrix towards renewable and clean energy sources. The solar park aims to comply with international climate change mitigation standards, aligning with worldwide efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and promote a more sustainable future.
In conclusion, the SunPower Project is not only designed to enhance Nicaragua’s energy supply but also plays a pivotal role in supporting the country's commitments to environmental sustainability and facilitating the transition to a cleaner, more responsible energy matrix.

The primary target group consists of small-scale farming households that own 3 to 5 cows, as they can eff ectively utilize biogas technology to meet their cooking needs. This initiative aims to tackle the pressing challenges of clean cooking, environmental degradation, and rural household energy dependence by providing sustainable cooking solutions for low-income households. description: The Programme of Activities (PoA) “TASC SOLUM - Sequestration and Optimised Landscapes Using Microbials” aims to improve the health of agricultural land in South Africa by using natural biostimulants to enhance soil carbon sequestration. TASC is including this Voluntary Project Activity within the PoA. The main goal of the project is to remove carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere and store it permanently in agricultural soils, which is good for the environment and can help reduce the effects of climate change by decreasing greenhouse gas emissions (GHG).Current intensive and high-input forms of agriculture are leading to biodiversity loss, soil erosion, poor water retention, decreased drought resilience, GHG emissions, decreased plant health and nutrition, and decreased soil health. Applying regenerative agricultural practices addresses these issues via several ways, including precision application of biological and chemical inputs, minimising soil disturbance, inter-cropping, cover cropping, and integrating livestock when possible. This project within the regenerative agriculture programme will focus on the precision application of biological and chemical inputs.

The regular case voluntary project activity (VPA) is providing household water filtration units for marginalized households in India living in rural, urban, semi-urban areas. The VPA is a part of POA and its real case VPA, which will contribute to the reduction of greenhouse gases and socio-economic progress for communities who are relying on unsafe drinking water sources and thus the objective of the VPA is to disseminate household water treatment units in Madhya Pradesh, India so that the rural communities living in remote hilly areas have increased access of safe drinking water for their daily use and thus increased living standard for the poor and marginalized people. 
The regular case VPA under the GS Programme of Activity provides safe household drinking water treatment solutions to marginalized households at free of cost and replace the usage of equivalent quantity of fuel wood in traditional three stone fire or any other conventional wood stoves which are inefficient and smoke-intensive and which would have been used to boil the water to make it safe for drinking purposes.

name: Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Western Kenya and Rift Valley
description:
The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Western Kenya and Rift Valley Kenya project is implemented in Kenya’s Elgeyo-Marakwet, Migori and Narok counties. Over several decades, these counties have experienced substantial deforestation and degradation because of poor agricultural practices, overgrazing and unsustainable demand for fuelwood. The scenario - the continued degradation of land and erosion of livelihood opportunities – will most likely continue to occur unless there is a substantial and additional intervention
The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in the Elgeyo-Marakwet, Migori and Narok counties in Kenya, involving more than 75,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include increased household income, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

name: Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Coastal Kenya
description:
The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Coastal Kenya project is implemented in Kenya’s coastal region, specifically in the Kwale and Kilifi counties. With an annual deforestation rate of 0.58%, Kenya faces significant forest loss, primarily driven by dependence on natural resources and extensive land degradation.  The primary causes of land degradation include unsustainable wood resource exploitation, the expansion of unsustainable cultivation practices, the spread of invasive species, pollution, and climate change.
The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in the Kwale and Kilifi counties in Kenya, involving more than 100,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include increased household income, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services.
The project builds on extensive experience in socio-economic development within the region.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

name: Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Malawi
description:
The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Malawi project is implemented in degraded agricultural landscapes in the in the Northern, Central and Southern Regions of the country. Over 90% of households in the country depend on natural resources and subsistence agriculture to meet their livelihoods, food and energy needs. Extensive clearing of forest and woodlands for fuelwood, followed by conversion to cropland, is driving a high annual deforestation rate of 1%.
The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in seven districts in Malawi involving more than 150,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include sustainable food production, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services.
The project will collaborate and align with the many organizations already established in the area to enhance long-term sustainability and ensure that implementation occurs in an efficient, locally appropriate, and acceptable manner.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals

description:
The Restore Africa: Restoring Landscapes and Livelihoods in Western Uganda project is implemented in degraded agricultural landscapes in the Western (Afromontane) highlands and pastoral rangelands of mid-Western Uganda. Over several decades, these regions have experienced substantial deforestation and degradation, poor agriculture practices, overgrazing, and an unsustainable demand for fuelwood. Climate change, population increases, poverty and lack of economic opportunities further exacerbate pressure on the land. 
The project focuses on establishment of new trees (e.g. through manual planting and broadcast seeding) as well as the improved management activities that enhance the natural regeneration of established root stock (e.g. through coppice management) in 24 districts in Western Uganda involving more than 200,000 small farmer households. The aim is to both sequester carbon as well as generate a broad set of environmental and socio-economic co-benefits through the implementation of sustainable agroforestry practices at a landscape scale. Co-benefits, based on the restoration of ecosystem functions, include sustainable food production, enhanced local livelihoods, increased gender equality and the improvement of ecosystem services.
The project will collaborate and align with the many organizations already established in the area to enhance long-term sustainability and ensure that implementation occurs in an efficient, locally appropriate, and acceptable manner.

name: Enabling Clean Energy Transitions Through BESS Integration
description: The project involves the deployment of a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) to store electricity generated from renewable energy sources such as solar or wind. The BESS enables time-shifting of renewable energy by storing surplus electricity during periods of low demand and discharging it during peak demand periods or grid stress events. This reduces the need for fossil fuel-based peaking power plants and supports grid stability and renewable energy integration. The system comprises battery, power conversion systems (inverters), battery management systems, and control software to optimize charging/discharging cycles. The project contributes to greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions by displacing grid electricity that would otherwise be generated from fossil fuels.

name: Canbaz Shipping Group Retrofit Project 1
description:
Shipping is a major source of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions globally, responsible for over 1 Gt of CO2eq in 2018, as per the International Maritime Organization's 2020 report. GHG emissions from international shipping are largely from fuel consumption in engines using fuel oil, diesel and some LNG. Energy efficiency improvements in shipping reduce fuel consumption in ships, leading to reduced CO2 emissions.

Canbaz Shipping Group (CSG) has made the decision to apply several energy efficiency retrofit measures to their fleet of ships. CSG is undertaking a Gold Standard project to apply for the issuance of carbon credits related to the retrofit energy efficiency measures installed and to-be-installed on a specific group of 6 vessels.

name: GS23280 VPA-1 RANOVOLA Water Program in Madagascar
description: The RANOVOLA project, building on infrastructure put in place by other HELVETAS initiatives, aims to ensure safe and sustainable access to clean water for the most vulnerable rural communities in Madagascar. The RANOVOLA project main objectives are to provide reliable access to clean water, improve public health by reducing the prevalence of waterborne diseases, strengthen the autonomy of local communities by collaborating with private operators to manage the operation and maintenance of the established infrastructure, support the ecological transition by limiting dependence on fossil fuels and firewood for water purification, and contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by acting on health, environmental, economic, and social fronts. The RANOVOLA project infrastructure will rely on two main technologies: 1) gravitational systems, using water sources located at higher altitudes to transport water to communities without the need for additional energy; and 2) solar pumping systems, utilizing boreholes to ensure a constant and economical water supply. In both cases, water treatment is carried out by filtration, chlorination, and iron removal. The operation and management of the infrastructure will be ensured by private operators, under a decentralized management model in compliance with Malagasy legal frameworks.
gsf_standards_version: Gold Standard for the Global Goals
poa_project_name: RANOVOLA Water Program

name: Chestnut Sustainable Restoration Megaton Project
description:
The United States is home to over 700 million acres of forestland, nearly 7.5% of the world’s forests, that provide clean water, recreation, and other life-sustaining resources to Americans. The importance of American forests to the global ecosystem and climate is central to the work of CC Project SPV, LLC (“Project Developer”), a US-based company that seeks to restore and conserve functional forestland throughout the United States for the primary purpose of increasing carbon sequestration. 

Using the Gold Standard Land Use and Forest Activities Requirements and A/R (afforestation and reforestation) methodologies, the Project Developer is implementing an afforestation project called the Chestnut Sustainable Restoration Megaton Project on multiple parcels of land within the United States. The Project Developer will be acquiring and leasing unproductive, intensively managed pasture and croplands to plant trees and restore diverse, native forests. The purpose of the project is to increase carbon stocks and sequester greenhouse gases while creating sustainably managed native forestland throughout the country. The Project Developer has extensive expertise in carbon project development and forest management. name: UHI “YUEDIAN 83”  Shipping Retrofit Project
description:
The Project comprises the application of one or more energy efficiency measures 
as retrofits to existing ships. The types of eligible retrofit measures include Design related measures、Propulsion measures、Machinery measures、Operating measures etc. These measures would reduce fossil fuel consumption and thereby reduce CO2 emissions. 
Since the ship in this project travels in international waters, shipping emissions and emissions reduction are not included in the GHG inventory of any country usually. The International Maritime Organisation (IMO, belonging to the UN) is responsible for setting commitments on emissions from ships, there is no Host Country for these 
projects. 
Moreover, there is no physical geographical location of the project activity. However, the ship has a unique identification number established by the IMO. As stated in Section “Baseline Methodology: Project Boundary” of the methodology “Retrofit Energy Efficiency Measures in Shipping”: “The spatial project boundary is the geographical location of project ships in which vessels are clearly identified by their unique IMO-Number.” 
.The proposed project is considered to be micro scale, since the expected emissions reductions are below 10,000 tCO2eq/year.

name: Ayyalur Livelihoods Project
description:
SEEDS Trust is a local NGO in the Tamil Nadu region of India that aims at improving livelihoods while restoring and protecting the environment in the Ayyalur landscape. SEEDS Trust, jointly with the Livelihoods Fund, developed the ‘Ayyalur Livelihoods Project’, which seeks to restore the degraded and over-exploited land which is suitable for a biodiverse spread of medicinal, nutritional, traditional, and productive trees, shrubs, and crops. The species that are native or endemic to this region are favored by the local community, who forage the land to provide for themselves and supply goods to the traditional alternative medicine sector of India. These foraging and farming practices tend to put extra strain on the women in these communities and is additionally characterized by unequal benefit sharing. The overall project objective is to positively impact the livelihoods of over 8,000 household smallholder farmers by planting over 4.5 million tree seedlings on 8,000 ha of land with an intercropping of nutritional crops and shrubs; with the goal to sequestrate 1,411 net tCO2e over the crediting period.

The main project activities are constituted of the following:

1. Agroforestry practices involve fruit and grain supplements, such as Mango, Tamarind, Jackfruit, and Millet.
2. Border trees provide timber resources, climate resilience, and canopy cover.
3. Apiculture trainings and supplies, along with the increased habitat of Grey Slender Loris, an IUCN near-threatened species.

The project implementation is closely tied to the local community and involves workshops and training for all members of the community working towards reaching the Sustainable Development Goals.
